title: The Regiment of the Palatinate
premise: In 1789 Strasbourg, Wren Joubert works her late father's type foundry inside a print shop, measuring life in what can be carried when the authorities come. A stranger named Elias Brandt arrives bearing letters in the unmistakable hand of Captain Aurel Voss — a Palatine officer officially dead for two years, whose regiment's mutiny was blamed on a massacre the victors' historians have already set in type. Wren and Elias must authenticate Voss's testimony, cut it into movable type, and print it before the censors and the century close over it, discovering along the way that Wren's father helped forge the original false record. The book ends on New Year's Eve 1799: the true account is in circulation across the Rhine, Voss alive but choosing exile, and Wren, having inherited both her father's guilt and his craft, stays to keep the press running as belonging finally means something she chose.
about_author: Quentin Halloran is the pen name of a former letterpress compositor who spent a decade restoring nineteenth-century printing equipment in Alsace before turning to fiction. His novels are known for their tactile precision and their obsession with how paper outlasts power.

chapters.title: The Weight of Sorts
chapters.summary: Wren Joubert's POV. In the Joubert foundry she sorts type by touch while soldiers requisition paper down the street; her father's death two years past left her the shop and its debts. She catalogs what could be carried if they come for her too. Emotional beat: quiet dread beneath competence.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Composing Stick
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Elias Brandt arrives at closing time asking for a printer who can match an old hand, producing letters signed by Captain Aurel Voss — a name Wren knows from her father's locked drawer of confiscated proofs. Emotional beat: recognition that unsettles everything she thought she inherited.

chapters.title: The Dead Man's Hand
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He explains he served under Voss, reported him dead after the Palatine regiment's massacre, then received these letters last month. He needs them authenticated and printed before the official history is bound into law. Emotional beat: grief sharpened into purpose.

chapters.title: What Father Kept Locked
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, alone at night. She opens her father's drawer and finds matrices cut to imitate another man's handwriting — including Voss's. Her father forged documents for the victors. Emotional beat: betrayal curdling into resolve.

chapters.title: Terms of Ink
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Wren offers Elias a bargain: she'll authenticate the letters against her father's matrices, but if the forgery implicates her family, the truth goes out whole or not at all. Elias, uneasy, agrees. Emotional beat: wary alliance sealed over ink-stained hands.

chapters.title: The Regiment of the Palatinate
chapters.summary: Elias's POV, told through his reading of Voss's letters aloud. The regiment refused an order to fire on petitioners; the massacre was committed by another unit and pinned on them; Voss fled rather than hang. Emotional beat: the scale of the lie becomes undeniable.

chapters.title: Censors at the Door
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. An inspector visits the shop on a routine license check, lingering over the new customer registered in the ledger. Wren realizes the victors are already hunting the letters' source. Emotional beat: fear made administrative.

chapters.title: Aurel
chapters.summary: Voss's POV, first time. Alive in a Rhineland safehouse, he wrote the letters knowing exposure means death, but his surviving soldiers' names deserve clearing. He trusts Elias because Elias once took a flogging meant for him. Emotional beat: duty inverted — living now serves the dead.

chapters.title: The Matrix Room
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Working by lamplight, she compares the letters to her father's forged matrices and confirms both truths: Voss is real, and her father cut the false confession that damned the regiment. Emotional beat: mourning a father she never truly knew.

chapters.title: Paper Is a Country
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He and Wren plan distribution through peddlers and river barges, and argue about whether printing truth or staying alive matters more. Something unspoken passes between them neither names. Emotional beat: love arriving disguised as argument.

chapters.title: The Widow's Testimony
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. They track down Margarethe Falk, widow of a hanged sergeant, who corroborates the letters and gives them her husband's final note. She asks only that his name be spelled correctly. Emotional beat: the cost of witness made human.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The army seizes half her lead stock 'for the war effort,' gutting her ability to cast enough type. She suspects the inspector tipped them deliberately. Emotional beat: the state tightening its grip one pound of metal at a time.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. With supplies short, they smuggle matrices and a small press out of the city to a mill upstream. Wren carries her father's forged matrices too — evidence, not inheritance. Emotional beat: flight that feels like becoming.

chapters.title: The Mill at Night
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Setting type by candlelight, she and Elias compose the first pages of the true account. A near-intimate moment breaks off when a patrol's lanterns sweep the lane. Emotional beat: tenderness interrupted by history.

chapters.title: The First Impression
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Two hundred copies come off the press; holding one, Elias weeps for the first time since the massacre. But a helper has vanished, and Wren fears he sold them out. Emotional beat: triumph shadowed by betrayal.

chapters.title: The Inspector's Ledger
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The inspector raids the mill but finds only cold type; however, he reveals he knew her father, and that the forgery order came from above — from the historian drafting the official record himself. Emotional beat: the conspiracy acquires a face.

chapters.title: Historian of the Victors
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss risks crossing the Rhine to confront the retired archivist who authored the false record, finding not a monster but a tired man who believed order required a clean story. Voss leaves him the widow's note. Emotional beat: contempt softening into terrible pity.

chapters.title: Confession in Type
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. To make the account unimpeachable, Wren includes her father's forged matrices as proof of the forgery itself — burning her family's name to save strangers'. Emotional beat: inheritance reclaimed through sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Century Turns Its Page
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. On the eve of the new year, the pamphlets flood Strasbourg; crowds read the sergeant's name aloud outside the garrison. The inspector, ordered to suppress it, instead resigns and lets the wagons pass. Emotional beat: the record slipping free of its keepers.

chapters.title: Voss's Choice
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Cleared but marked, Voss refuses reinstatement and chooses exile across the Atlantic, telling Elias that some men belong to no regiment after what regiments have done. Emotional beat: survival without homecoming.

chapters.title: New Year's Eve, 1799
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At midnight, church bells and press clatter mingle; Elias asks her to come with him to the Rhineland presses, and she says she'll go — but the foundry ships with her, lock, stock, and matrix. Emotional beat: love chosen freely, duty redefined.

chapters.title: The Standing Form
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, epilogue. Years later, a restored Joubert & Brandt press prints schoolbooks containing the corrected history; Wren keeps one locked drawer, now holding her own honest records. She measures the world still in what can be carried — and finds it heavier, and hers. Emotional beat: belonging earned and kept.
